title: Peek at the last bytes
description: record.dat ends with an eight-character trailer, and the file has no line ending after it. Print exactly the last eight bytes of the file and nothing else. Example: a file ending in ABCDEFGHIJ, asking for the last three bytes -> HIJ. The count has to be measured in bytes rather than lines, which the command does not do by default.
objective: Practise taking the end of a file by byte count instead of line count.
check:
if ! printf 'END-7F3A' | cmp -s - "$CMM_STDOUT"; then
  echo "Expected exactly the eight bytes END-7F3A, with no line ending. Got:"
  cat -et "$CMM_STDOUT"
  echo
  echo "(A line end shows as \$ above.)"
  exit 1
fi

title: Keep only the bottom of the output
description: app.log mixes INFO and ERROR lines. Print the two most recent ERROR lines, meaning the last two lines containing ERROR, in the order they appear in the file, and nothing else. Example: the lines ERROR a, INFO b, ERROR c, ERROR d, INFO e -> ERROR c, ERROR d. The limit has to apply to the matching lines, not to the file itself, since the end of the file may not be errors at all.
objective: Practise limiting another command's output to its last few lines.
setup:
printf 'INFO boot
ERROR disk full
INFO retry
ERROR timeout
ERROR refused
INFO recovered
INFO idle
INFO idle
' > app.log
check:
expected=$(printf 'ERROR timeout\nERROR refused')
if [ "$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected the last two ERROR lines, in file order:"
  echo "$expected"
  echo "Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi

title: Everything after the header
description: report.txt starts with three header lines, followed by the data. Print every line from line 4 through to the end of the file, in file order, and nothing else. Example: the lines h1, h2, h3, x, y -> x, y. The file grows from day to day, so the command has to say where to start reading, not how many lines to keep: your command is run a second time against a longer file.
objective: Practise printing a file from a given line onward to skip a known header.
check:
expected=$(printf 'mon 12\ntue 7\nwed 19\nthu 3')
if [ "$(cat "$CMM_STDOUT")" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "Expected every line from line 4 to the end, in file order:"
  echo "$expected"
  echo "Got:"
  cat "$CMM_STDOUT"
  exit 1
fi
printf 'fri 8\n' >> report.txt
expected=$(printf '%s\nfri 8' "$expected")
if [ "$(bash "$CMM_COMMAND" 2>/dev/null)" != "$expected" ]; then
  echo "That output was right for this file, but the command broke once the file gained a line: it should start at line 4, not keep a fixed number of lines from the end."
  exit 1
fi
